The first thing my father labeled was the label maker.

He printed LABEL MAKER on a strip of white plastic, trimmed the corners with nail scissors, and stuck it to the gray casing just above the trigger. Then he held it at arm’s length.

“There,” he said.

My mother looked up from her crossword.

“Thank God. I thought it was a duck.”

This was the kind of marriage they had: he secured the world against misunderstanding, and she introduced a little misunderstanding wherever she could.

By the time I left for college, nearly everything in the house had acquired a name. EXTENSION CORD. FLOUR. SPARE KEYS. The drawers in his workshop bore increasingly specialized descriptions: WOOD SCREWS, MACHINE SCREWS, SCREWS—UNCERTAIN.

That last drawer was my mother’s favorite.

“A drawer for doubt,” she said. “Every home should have one.”

After she died, the labels multiplied.

UPSTAIRS LIGHT SWITCH.

WATER SHUTOFF.

POLICY DOCUMENTS.

He labeled the backs of photographs, which was sensible, and then the fronts, which was less so. Under a picture of my mother standing beside a lake, he put ELAINE, LAKE SUPERIOR, 1987.

I knew her name. I knew the lake. I remembered the trip: rain for six days, a cabin that smelled of damp matches, my father insisting the weather was about to break.

When I asked why the label had to go on the front, he said, “You shouldn’t have to turn something over to know what it is.”

I let it go.

He lived alone for another eleven years.

When he died, I took two weeks off work and drove home with cardboard boxes folded flat in the trunk. I had made a spreadsheet. There were columns for keep, donate, sell, discard.

For the first few days, I was efficient.

The towels went to the animal shelter. The canned food went to a church. A man with enormous hands bought the drill press and carried it out as gently as if it were asleep.

I found seven tape measures.

I found the receipt for a toaster purchased before I was born.

In the drawer marked SCREWS—UNCERTAIN, I found a tooth.

An adult molar, wrapped in tissue.

For several minutes I stood in the workshop holding it, hoping some piece of information would arrive to make it an ordinary possession.

None did.

I put it back.

On the fourth day, I began peeling labels from things I wanted to keep.

The lettering on the sugar bowl came off cleanly. The label on the sewing tin left a sticky rectangle. On the bottom of a brass lamp, beneath the expected LIVING ROOM LAMP, I found another strip.

ELAINE LIKED THIS ONE.

I sat down.

I had assumed the labels were there to help me empty the house. Now I wondered how many I had thrown away.

There were others.

Behind the kitchen clock: TEN MINUTES FAST ON PURPOSE.

Inside his good coat: WORE TO YOUR GRADUATION.

Under the small blue dish by the telephone: SHE BOUGHT THIS AFTER WE QUARRELED. I DON’T REMEMBER WHY WE QUARRELED.

His machine had no lowercase letters. Even this came out looking like an instruction.

I began examining everything before I put it in a box.

The dining table had a label underneath, where I used to hide during thunderstorms.

YOU THOUGHT WE COULDN’T SEE YOUR FEET.

On the ladder: THIRD RUNG LOOSE. ALSO I AM SORRY ABOUT THE TREEHOUSE.

I remembered being furious about the treehouse. He had promised to build it one summer, then worked Saturdays through August. By September I had stopped asking. When he offered the following spring, I told him I was too old.

I turned the ladder over and checked the rung. It was loose.

That evening I called my sister.

“Did you know about the labels?”

“Obviously.”

“No. The other ones.”

She was quiet for a moment.

“Look in the freezer,” she said.

At the back, beneath a bag of peas gone solid with frost, was a foil package.

YOUR MOTHER’S LAST GOOD SOUP.

“Don’t eat it,” my sister said.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“I know. I just needed to say it.”

We stayed on the phone while I cleaned the freezer. Eventually I put the soup in the trash, then took it out again. My sister listened to the foil crackle.

“You can do it tomorrow,” she said.

On my last morning, I found the label maker in his desk. There was still tape in it.

I tried to think of something worth putting on the house before I left. Every sentence sounded either too grand or like something he would have corrected.

So I packed it.

Months later, my daughter found it in our kitchen drawer.

“What’s this?”

“A label maker.”

“What does it do?”

I showed her. She considered the available world, then slowly pressed out a word, turning the dial with both hands.

She peeled away the backing and stuck the label on my shirt.

DAD.

“There,” she said.
